name: Zane Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck team and keep a folded paper map beside the controls. I walk a route before the first run, check radio calls, then listen for a loose coupling when the truck turns under load.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing my crew can get the job done without taking a shortcut around a hazard. The rotation wears me down, but the pay is high and I have more than six months saved, so I do not have to chase every new thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the board can sort routine notes if it leaves the route checks alone. I still want a person in the cab when a haul road changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly operating equipment, so a small improvement to routine notes does not look like a pay threat to me. I have eight months saved and plenty of mines nearby, and I am not looking for a reason to change a routine that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same crew rotation and check the board's notes against the folded map and radio. If the notes stayed accurate for a month, I would let the dispatcher use them for routine handovers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work and income in this mild case. I would rather spend my attention on the route than on an update that saves the office a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you ask the dispatcher to stop using the new notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a closure call or soft shoulder were missing, I would stop the truck and have the dispatcher check it. I would write the correction on the folded map before the next shift took over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would you try it before deciding whether it helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare one full month of notes with the control-room log. If the crew still had to rewrite the same warnings, I would ask to return to the paper handover.

say: I would let the board sort routine notes if it leaves **route checks** alone.
I still want a person in the cab when **roads change**.
think: I think my operating job and pay look **secure** in this mild case.
My eight months saved mean I need not **rush a change**.
do: Keep the **same crew rotation** and check notes against the folded map.
Compare one month of handovers with the **control-room log**.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own work and income in this version.
S0.quote: I still want a person in the cab when a haul road changes.
fieldNote: Zane relies on **route checks** and physical listening rather than a screen.
His **savings and local alternatives** make a mild change financially manageable.
He proposes a **month-long comparison** before accepting routine automation.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and compare notes with the folded map
Wait one month before deciding whether to use notes routinely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the mine can use software for booking and paperwork, but the crew still needs a clear handover. A paper map and a clear radio call still matter on a night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving job seems less exposed than the planning work, but I lead some of that planning between runs. I do not use AI, and I would only learn a new system if someone showed it working on our road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to show me the route planner on a regular shift, with the paper map beside it. If another experienced driver could verify the result, I would use the planner for that task and keep checking the route myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because lead planning could change, even if the truck work remains. My income looks safe for now, and I have savings to take a course if the mine posts a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What change would you look for in your rota or pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for fewer lead shifts or a lower allowance on my pay slip. If either changed, I would ask the foreman whether the new system caused it before deciding to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner and a driver disagree about a route, what would you want to happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the driver to pause and check the road with the radio operator. The machine can offer a route, but the person in the cab must be able to reject it when the ground says otherwise.

say: I would use software for paperwork, but keep a **clear handover**.
I would keep the **paper map** and radio call on night shift.
think: I think my driving job is less exposed than **planning work**.
I would learn a system only after it works on **our road**.
do: Ask the foreman to demonstrate the **route planner** beside the paper map.
Use it only after another driver **verifies the result**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about planning tasks, though my income looks safe now.
S1.quote: A paper map and a clear radio call still matter on a night shift.
fieldNote: Zane resists new systems until another driver **verifies them** on the road.
His **lead planning duties** create some concern, but not an immediate income threat.
He wants operators to keep **route authority**.

steps.text: Wait for the foreman to demonstrate the route planner on site
Keep using the paper map and radio while driving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives first, and robots for hands-on work follow about three years later. I would ask the mine to show which paid training courses lead to actual vacancies before it changes the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the truck job could be at risk by 2031, even if AGI first handles the lead's paperwork. I have more than six months saved and many other mines nearby, but I do not want to wait until the machines are in the pit to learn another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask a mechanic to walk me through the paid heavy-equipment maintenance course the mine uses, then take its first unit if the trainer explains the job. In 2029, after AGI arrives, I would apply for a physical inspection job only if the employer named the wage and the work involved checking or repairing equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could replace the main task I am paid for within five years. I have time and money to prepare, but I would rather learn a proven trade than pretend the current job is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the maintenance job is mostly records or planning that AGI can already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not treat the title as protection; AGI can do those thinking tasks too. I would ask whether the work is physical and how many paid posts remain once robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine cannot name the pay or the number of posts, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my haul-truck job while checking the other mines and their course schedules. I would not leave a high-paying role for a maintenance label without a written offer.

say: I would say thinking AI comes first and robots follow **three years later**.
I would ask for training linked to **real vacancies**.
think: I think the truck job could be at risk by **2031**.
My savings and local options give me **time to prepare**.
do: Take the first unit of a paid **heavy-equipment course** after a mechanic explains the work.
In 2029, apply only for physical work with a **named wage**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because robots could replace my main task within five years.
S2.quote: I have more than six months saved and many other mines nearby, but I do not want to wait until the machines are in the pit to learn another trade.
fieldNote: Zane connects the robot date to **his main paid task**.
Savings and nearby mines provide time, but he rejects a **last-minute retraining plan**.
He distinguishes physical maintenance from **records AGI handles**.

steps.text: Take the first paid heavy-equipment maintenance course unit
Apply for a physical inspection job with a named wage in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the mine time to train people before it changes its plans. A robot date gives me time, but it does not promise a paid job afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have eight years before robots are expected, which is enough time to learn mechanical inspection while I earn a truck wage. I do not want a desk job after AGI, and I would need to know how many hands-on positions last beyond 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete a paid apprenticeship in equipment inspection before 2031 and keep my truck qualification current. In 2032, after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical maintenance work only if the employer stated its pay and expected end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have time to prepare, but I cannot know how many people the mine will keep. I would stay on the truck while learning instead of leaving for an uncertain role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you that the apprenticeship is worth the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mechanic to show me an ordinary inspection and what a new worker earns. I would also check whether two nearby mines use the same certificate before I paid for any extra course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if inspection work is a short bridge before robots arrive, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it if the wage covered my costs and gave me time to apply elsewhere before 2034. If it did not, I would keep the truck job and continue checking other openings.

say: I would say five years gives the mine time to **train people**.
I would not treat a robot date as **a paid job promise**.
think: I have eight years to learn while **earning a truck wage**.
I need to know how many physical roles last beyond **2034**.
do: In 2032, apply only with a stated **wage and end date**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I have time, but mine staffing remains unknown.
S3.quote: A robot date gives me time, but it does not promise a paid job afterward.
fieldNote: Zane views eight years as **training time**, not job security.
He rejects desk planning as a **fallback after AGI**.
He checks **job duration and pay** before moving.

steps.text: Complete the paid equipment-inspection apprenticeship before 2031
Apply for physical maintenance work with a stated end date in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the mine to use the lead time for paid training and a clear plan for each crew. We need years to organize training, but no one should call a temporary post secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 40 when robots are expected, and my pay and savings give me time to learn a trade. I would still ask whether hands-on maintenance work exists after 2039 before I make a long-term move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shift while checking the mine's equipment course and who hires its graduates. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would compare the physical job openings and wages before changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my income and job look secure for years, and I can build a second skill before then. I would not leave steady work until a real vacancy had clear duties and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you need before taking a maintenance post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the physical work includes, what it pays and how long the employer expects to need people. I would want a written answer about whether the role continues after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the employer cannot say whether the role lasts after 2039, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current job and ask nearby mines for their training schedules. I would wait for a clear job and wage before moving.

say: I would ask for paid training and a **crew-by-crew plan**.
I would not call a temporary post **secure**.
think: My pay and savings give me **time to learn**.
I will check physical jobs after **2039** before moving.
do: Join the **union transition group** and request paid courses and job forecasts.
In 2037, compare physical vacancies and **wages** before moving to another mine.
feel: I feel **calm** because work and income look secure for years.
S4.quote: We need years to organize training, but no one should call a temporary post secure.
fieldNote: Zane sees the long warning as **time to prepare** while earning.
He wants written details on **physical duties**, wages and job length.
His savings let him wait for a real vacancy rather than **rush**.

steps.text: Join the union group requesting paid courses and job forecasts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reach the truck work within five years. Paid training, a clear list of vacancies and enough notice would help me choose another job without giving up a steady wage too early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want to know the wage and the length of the job before I leave my crew. I can learn a trade when I see the work, but I will not move on a promise alone.

headlineQuote: I want to know the wage and the length of the job before I leave my crew.
portrait: Zane Evans is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
He earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of expenses saved.
Plenty of local mines give him **other options** if the roster changes.
He **avoids AI tools** and learns only after seeing a trade work in practice.
He favors **clear job duties**, wages and dates over an uncertain move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves about five years before robots could change Zane's truck work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, clear vacancies and enough notice would help Zane choose another job without rushing.
